speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement concerning the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. This act came into force on January 1, 1963 and contains the provision that the minister may take legal action against firms or unions which have not reported by July 1, 1963, for fiscal periods ending in the calendar year 1962. Similar enforcement provisions apply to firms and unions which have not reported within six months after the end of succeeding fiscal periods.
However, since this legislation is new and some firms and labour unions are experiencing problems in supplying all the information required, I wish to announce that I do not intend to undertake legal proceedings against firms or unions which make the required returns before October 1, 1963. This should provide ample time for reporting.
After all returns for the first year have been received and analysed, it may be possible in the light of experience to introduce changes which would reduce reporting difficulties of firms and unions.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY TO MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY TO MINISTER OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
As they will affect the handling of questions in the house, may I take this opportunity to inform hon. members of certain administrative changes, effective as of July 1, with respect to civil emergency planning.
This program, as members will recall, is carried on at the federal level by various departments and agencies of the government and has been co-ordinated by the emergency measures organization in the privy council office. An order in council, P.C. 1959-656, is the basis of the arrangement in effect up to this time, with the Prime Minister and the Ministers of National Defence, National Health and Welfare and Justice being those specifically allocated various responsibilities by the order.
The government has decided to consolidate arrangements and to bring about a closer degree of co-ordination among the emergency measures organization, the civil defence college and the emergency supplies planning branch in the Department of Defence Production. Pursuant to the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, order in council P.C. 1963-993, a copy of which I am now tabling, transfers the responsibility for the emergency measures organization from the Prime Minister to the Minister of Defence Production. The order also transfers responsibility for the civil defence college from the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the Minister of Defence Production to be exercised through the emergency measures organization. The director of the emergency measures organization will report direct to the Minister of Defence Production.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BARBADOS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR SUPPLY OF POLIO VACCINE AND RESPIRATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will wish to be informed of action which is being taken to meet an urgent need in the island of Barbados, where there has been a serious outbreak of polio. According to information received through the British colonial office, 38 cases of polio were notified from March 27 to June 6. Mass vaccination is now in progress using oral trivalent. A total of 61,483 doses are required, and the government of Barbados asked whether Canada would be prepared to assist in providing 50,000 doses and one or two respirators.
The government has now agreed that the vaccine should be made available and it will be carried free of charge by T.C.A. on its regular scheduled flight tomorrow, July 3. The estimated cost of $5,500 for the vaccine will be provided in the supplementary estimates of the Department of External Affairs. The provision of respirators involves some complication, but the matter is being looked into immediately.
I am sure all members of the house will join in the hope that these measures may help in meeting the serious emergency which has arisen in the island.

Mr. Speaker, my question of personal privilege derived from the fact that several contradictory decisions on your part as well as several answers from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) prevented us from obtaining information to which we are entitled.
On several occasions, in fact on five different occasions, I asked the Minister of Finance what were the administrative difficulties which compelled him to withdraw the 30 per cent tax on sales of Canadian shares to non-residents. As a matter of fact, as stated on page 1373 of the official report for June 20, 1963, I asked the following question:
Could the Minister of Finance tell us what are the administrative difficulties which have compelled him to withdraw that tax?
At that time your decision was as follows, as stated on the same page of the report:
I regret to inform the hon. member for Lapointe that his last supplementary question was in the nature of an argument.
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that my question was effectively a question and not an argument.
Again, as recorded on page 1527 of the Hansard for June 25, I asked the same question, and you ruled as follows:
-I suggest to the hon. member that he raise this question during the budget debate-
Mr. Speaker, I asked the question during the budget debate. After the conclusion of that debate I asked the question again and you stated then that you had already settled the matter, and that you had not allowed me to ask the question on the orders of the day because it was during the budget debate, and now that the budget debate is over, you ruled it out for a third time.
Mr. Speaker, I asked the question for the fifth time on June 27, and you ruled then that the matter should be postponed until the debate on the budget resolutions. As recorded in Hansard for Wednesday, June 19, in the first column of page 1321, the Minister of Finance stated the following:

Pending a solution, the government proposes to withdraw paragraph 11 of the budget resolution respecting the Excise Tax Act.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, there are three contradictions. First, you did not let us ask such a question during the budget debate and you asked us to wait until after the debate. Then, you ruled it out of order because you had already postponed its consideration. You referred it until the examination of the budget resolutions and then the Minister of Finance withdrew it from the budget resolutions.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, on several instances the Minister of Finance stated that he would consider the question during the budget debate. Indeed, as reported in the right hand column of page 1373 of Hansard for June 20, he said this:
Mr. Speaker, I would be glad to go into that but, although I am not an expert in the rules, I suggest that is a matter that should be taken up in the debate.
It is the Minister of Finance himself who stated that the matter should be taken up during the debate.
On the same page of Hansard, the Prime Minister intimated that the question should be discussed during the debate.
I raised the question on another instance, and the Minister of Finance again said that it should be examined during the debate. I carefully read over the whole speech the Minister of Finance made on June 24 during the budget discussion and nowhere did I find a mention of the administrative difficulties which motivated the withdrawal of that 30 per cent tax on the sale of Canadian shares to foreign interests.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, that is, first of all the contradictions I found in former Hansards, and the promise of the Minister of Finance to mention it when discussing the budget, whereas he made no allusion to it in his speech, I think it is in order to ask the Minister of Finance that question and to get an answer from him on such an important and urgent matter, which implies very serious considerations.
Mr. Speaker, as several ministers including the Prime Minister have joined efforts to try and protect the Minister of Finance, I think it is one of my privileges, as well as those of the house, to see that the question be declared in order, so that the Minister of Finance may have a chance of answering it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he would refer to the Canadian wheat board my question regarding slow deliveries of wheat from points in the eastern half of Saskatchewan. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I should like to refer to some questions asked in my absence concerning the announcement made by the Prime Minister on uranium. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked the Acting Prime Minister-who I believe said I would answer these questions on my return-as to the financial commitment made by the government in this stockpiling program. As hon. members will have noted from the Prime Minister's statement, the government said that it is prepared to buy and stockpile the quantities of uranium that will enable certain mines to maintain present employment until July 1, 1964, at prices that will cover the operating costs of the mines to that date.
There are a number of uncertainties involved. First of all it will be necessary to find out how much uranium will be produced by these mines in order to keep them operating until July 1, 1964, and it will also be necessary to negotiate the prices that will cover the operating costs of the mines. Therefore it is impossible to give a very firm figure. However, I have consulted with Eldorado about the order of magnitude, and I can reply to the hon. gentleman that it will probably be of the order of $20 million. This figure is not exact, and is of course subject to negotiation. As the Minister of Finance said in reply to a later question, as and when these negotiations are completed the proposals will be put before parliament for approval including a supplementary estimate for the purpose.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked the Acting Prime Minister whether the assistance forthcoming under this announced plan would be applicable only to the uranium companies named in Ontario and not to those in Saskatchewan operating in the Beaver-lodge and Uranium City areas. As I understand it, there are two mines at Beaverlodge; Gunnar, which is closing because of lack of ore, and Eldorado which has already stretched out its contract so that it will be operating beyond July 1, 1964, which is the period covered by the announced stockpiling for the

Inquiries of the Ministry other mines. So in fact, nothing needs to be done or could be done with respect to those mines.
Finally the hon. member for Springfield directed a supplementary question to the Acting Prime Minister and asked whether he would investigate and report to the house on what the private uranium producing companies were doing in view of the fact that they have received $2J billion in government contracts and had "made some $400 million in profits".
Mr. Speaker, these contracts were not in effect with the Canadian government. Eldorado was buying the uranium on behalf of the United States and British governments, and was simply the conduit pipe through which the uranium flowed. I do not really feel under these circumstances it would be required of any minister of the Canadian government to be either a critic of or an apologist for these uranium companies.

speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce having to do with the decision to stockpile uranium at a cost of $20 million to the Canadian people. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ALLEGED CREATION OF CONFUSION AND CHAOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the tradition of parliament this motion gives an opportunity to hon. members to bring to the attention of government matters of national or local interest that are deserving of the immediate consideration of the government of the day. Today I do not intend to speak at length. I am going to devote myself to dealing particularly with one matter and on the basis of that matter to move an amendment.
It is the accepted principle of parliament that the opposition has a responsibility to bring before the people as a whole those matters which are of transcendent importance and which require, as I said a moment ago, the earliest possible attention. That is the essence of the concept of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, a concept which arose over 125 years ago, and gives to the opposition the responsibility of placing before parliament
Alleged Confusion in Economic Policies matters regarding which it believes the government has been in default. It must be reasonable; it must be responsible, but it also must be fearless in placing the viewpoint of the people before the representatives of the people.
This has been the attitude of this opposition during the present session. We have endeavoured, by examination and cross-examination, to bring about changes which in our view are necessary. No government has a monopoly of doing things with perfection. I know from my own experience over the years that often I have been strongly in support of a change that I believed was necessary only to learn, in retrospect, during the course of an examination in the house and the weighing of the issues by those on the other side of the house, that there were two sides to the question.
Three weeks ago tomorrow the budget was introduced. Of course I cannot deal with the budget in any way directly, but there are some matters which come within the purview of the right of an opposition at a time like this. For instance, I could not deal with a matter that appears in today's Gazette. I find that Mr. John Meyer, financial editor, writes an article headed "Sales Tax Extension Must be Withdrawn". This would be an improper stand for me to take; that is, to bring it before the house, laudable though the objectives be and although I agree with the thought expressed by the writer.
I look back a few months, sir, and I think of what the members of the government said then and of the changes that have taken place in the intervening months. Do you recall how they spoke with such authority? "Let us get the economy moving", they said. They did not say which way. The promises they held forth of expansion in our development have been proven, in the light of subsequent events, a great hoax perpetrated on the people. Indeed, there is no one on that side of the house who last year prated of Canada's economic deterioration who would dare say today that the increase in the national product of 8 per cent is going to be equalled this year. Indeed, they are down 3 per cent below that.
They had all the answers, Mr. Speaker. Give them an opportunity; give them but 60 days, and all would be well. Promissory notes carry with them three days of grace. We will give them far more grace than that. We have done so already, and we know on the basis of what has taken place that the promises of a few months ago have in the light of experience become the mirages of today.
Can we get information? We had an example today. I doubt that in the history of
1736	HOUSE OF
Alleged, Confusion in Economic Policies this country a government has had its stock fall faster in a period of three months than this government has. The reason is that the plans of yesterday, those that we know of, have become not the programs of today but the hopes of tomorrow. There is no excuse for what they have done in the fact that they were rushed, that they created their own boobytrap in the 60 days. They had the answers, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Three years ago, four years ago. They cannot put the blame on the Minister of Finance. I feel sorry for him sometimes because one would think he was to be made the scapegoat. speechtext:
Now they would have us believe that the reason they brought before the house plans ill digested, ill thought out and ill timed lies in the fact that they have been in a rush. It is not for me today to go back and read "Troubled Canada" but, sir, all these things that have been before parliament in the last few weeks were set out in great detail or in magnificent outline.
In the short time that parliament has been in session we have found how difficult it is to get information. The Minister of Agriculture is generous in this regard. When we ask him we get information. The other ministers, however, have much to learn from him. The kind of answers we have been getting have been nothing but a series of postponements, procrastinations and promises of future action.
I heard over the radio yesterday that parliament is going to sit without a summer recess unless the opposition passes the legislation that the government has placed before the house. Surely that is a strange view. We will support legislation that we believe to be beneficial. We will weigh the arguments pro and con in regard to that legislation. But let me make it clear right now that we are not going to be intimidated into supporting resolutions that will be brought before the house just because the government brings them forth and regardless of the ill effects upon the Canadian people, which are already apparent.
I mentioned a moment ago the hopes, and we look back to what the Minister of Finance said; because after all he became


the self appointed tribune of the people. He carried the message. He told us what was wrong. He told us what we needed. I do not blame him. Some people are so self appointed that they can do that. He said that these things should be done. On February 28 he used certain words, and I point out to those across the way who may be thinking of interrupting that they said "This is right; we can follow him and his ideas and bring about a new Canada". This is what he said on February 28:
What Canada needs is a government that knows where it is going-

-is prepared to make decisions and has enough pride and energy to push those policies through to a conclusion.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to think of the record since this house opened. Measure it on the basis of the program set out by the Minister of Finance. A government that knows where it is going? When questions were asked today as to what the government is going to do about the sales tax on production machinery and building materials the answer was in effect the answer we have had for several weeks. "Wait and see; some time I will give you an answer". Today in answer to the hon. member for Waterloo North the minister went as far as to say "Next Monday".
Is this the directional planning, so-called, that Canada needed? Where is Canada going? On the basis of what has taken place in the last few weeks and the uncertainty of this government, Canada's economy is going to be undermined in every part of the land. That is not my view alone. That is the view of Canadians in every part of Canada. Indeed, the Postmaster General should be able to have a healthy profit in his department if postage is paid on all the messages being received by the government which are critical of its actions and demanding action.

speechtext: It could not be worse, anyway.

speechtext:
I believe the minister is right. The scripture says, Mr. Speaker, "Out of the mouths of babes". I must say I am in agreement there. It could not be much worse, though I will say that on the basis of what is taking place with regard to the economy in every part of Canada it is the purpose of the opposition to assure that it shall not be worse. That is what we are setting out to do, and this has been the reason for the questions we have asked.

Let us get the picture. The government is asking for a vote of supply. They promised- I remember hearing this over and over again -to restore confidence. I should like to find any part of Canada where on every hand, among those supporting their party and those opposed as well, there has ever been a like loss of confidence in such large measure and in so short a time. Restore confidence? Go to the markets of New York. Go to the markets of London. Find out what their reaction is. They cannot understand the philosophy of the government. They do not understand the philosophy that activated it in bringing into effect the promise of measures that cannot but destroy, or certainly undermine, the economy.
Sir, they said we overspent, and they said they would balance the budget. They changed that a bit in the last election and said it would take a little time. It will, at the rate they are increasing expenditures. They will never be able to do it on the basis of the extra expenditures they have already undertaken since assuming power.
In every part of the nation the economy is in disarray. There is uncertainty due to the vacillation of a government that makes a great decision with a fanfare of trumpets one day and reverses it the next. The government speaks of anti-Americanism as though the opposition had a monopoly of it, but it puts into effect measures that out anti-Americanize anything ever introduced in this house previously. It has alienated the image of Canada abroad.
What about the various industries of Canada? What about the construction industry? In every part of the nation the hope was for an expanded investment on the part of Canadians everywhere. That was a few weeks ago; but today the industry is in the doldrums, fearful of the consequences of acts of legislative assassination that it faces.
Government plans, so eloquently placed before the country, have brought a fear to the people of the nation that has never been known before. Mr. Speaker, I am not discussing the budget; I shall refuse to do that. What I am doing is discussing the state of the economy.
Just go to any part of Canada and take a poll of the people you meet. Ask them what is their reaction. They cannot understand that on parliament hill, when incentives should be assured in order to bring about further expansion of an expanding economy which the government inherited, the brakes are being put on. Why is this? Yet, with the people afraid and angered, and with employment in grave danger, when we ask the answer is, "I have nothing to add; I have nothing to say." 28902-5-111

They used to say of the government, of which I had the honour to be the head, that business thought we did not take the proper attitude to it. Well, I would ask some of the ministers across the aisle to go to Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax or Vancouver and let the people talk to them. They cannot understand it. They ask: What manner of people are these?
When the government, with fearlessness, introduced the 30 per cent takeover tax there was strong objection from the powerful. Indeed the retreat from it was almost a riot. But when we ask for information about what is going to be done we cannot get it. Are construction industries to be held up because of the refusal of the government to explain the sales tax? What of the provinces? Mr. Lesage has given his views in this regard. The government used to quote him frequently; it does not do it so much any more. What about the municipalities and schoolboards across Canada?
What about the businesses that planned for development? Is the inertia of the government to be permitted by parliament to interfere with the continuing growth of the nation? We ask for information but we are answered by silence, by being pushed aside, or by some new gimmick or press propaganda wherein some new policy is announced.
I have just mentioned Mr. Lesage. He is disturbed, as are Canadians everywhere. In fact he said this:
This is very serious, especially when one realizes to what point school completions, municipalities and hydro will be affected; more than $5 million in 12 months in tax, nothing but tax, 11 per cent.
The Canadian construction association has said the industry will lose $100 million in construction work that was ready to be undertaken. The Canadian magazine owners and the press cannot understand this tax, and I would remind the house that we brought in and placed on the statute books of this country the right of freedom of the press. Where is the freedom of the press today? It is subject to an imposition of tax on the machinery that produces the things which provide education for the people.
The O'Leary commission said we were in danger of losing Canada's identity because Canadian magazines could not compete with imported magazines. If they could not compete at that stage, how will they compete in the face of this tax impost on machinery? Every field of national effort cannot understand the purpose of a government throwing monkey wrenches into the machinery of an advancing economy.

Alleged Confusion in Economic Policies
The government speaks of employment, but what it has done in the last few weeks, if it is able to put it into effect, will bring about new levels of unemployment at a time when we had the situation in reasonable hand. Canadians as a whole are asking us in parliament, "Why do you do this; why crucify Canadian development?" We cannot get the answers. We are being put off. We are advised that next week or the week after there will be announcements; but every day that this is said the Canadian economy is left in uncertainty and detriment is being done to it.
Hon. members of the government used to speak of the necessity of building a proCanadian attitude. That was their policy. But in his book the Minister of Finance said:
In our view there are definite limits as to what should be done about this matter, and compulsion and discrimination should certainly not be countenanced.
That is, against foreign investment. I will not go into the particulars as to what they have done in this regard. Sir, it is a serious situation for Canada. These hon. gentlemen opposite must not have the same correspondence that we do. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) was out west: I wonder what he reported back as to the reaction. Two of the ministers have been down in the maritimes, I understand; some ministers have been in Quebec and others in Ontario. Everywhere the question is, "Why are you doing this to us?" and the answer is, "Because Mr. Gordon told me so". Every one of them must take the responsibility; they are together on this.
Sir, I am not going to refer to newspapers, unless I am forced to do so; but everywhere across this nation there is the idea that this government is off the rails in its economic thinking. The average Canadian cannot understand why this has been done. He sees the threat to his position; he already anticipates losing the job that he has. He sees great projects being held up. Why? Because the government refuses to act. I come back to those words of the Minister of Finance:
What Canada needs is a government that knows where it is going.
Certainly I know where Canada is going unless something is done in this regard. The Minister of Finance said we need a government that knows where it is going and is prepared to make decisions. What decisions have been made? The decisions on matters that affect the economic future of Canada have taken second place to decisions that provide for appointments and the like. Everywhere across Canada people are asking that something be done in this regard. I received a telegram today from the chairman of the Ontario council of the national house builders association which reads:

In this position I must again point out the alarming impact of sales tax on house building materials. This is abundantly evident in sales cancellations, indefinite postponement of starts across this province with lay-offs now becoming evident. I urge you ascertain the chaotic situations and uncertainty in this industry which are having serious repercussions upon unemployment and reinstate exemptions to this important industry.
That is signed by Eric Johnson, chairman of the Ontario council of the national house builders association. Mining companies are hit by it in regard to their machinery and the necessity of providing the projects necessary to permit of mining taking place. Mines will have to close down because of this new tax. Secondary manufacturing in Canada has received a setback by the threat of the kind of action this government has in mind. It is because of these things that from everywhere members of all parties are being asked to do their part to save Canadians from this government; that is what we are being asked to do. The Orillia Packet-Times summed the whole matter up in one editorial. I am not going into particulars, again, unless I am asked to do so. This article is headed "Gordon finds that 'ruin' looks better from inside" and it says this:
Stranger still is the new government's financial review of 1962; the year in which Canada was supposed to be headed for ruin. It turns out that 1962 was not only a pretty good year, after all, but was actually one of the best ever for this country, with a rate of economic growth and activity that the new government would be only too pleased to sustain, let alone improve on.
In other words, the economic disaster Canadians were warned about so frequently a few months ago, existed only in the minds of the Liberal party publicists. There was, in fact, no crisis and certainly the Liberals had no drastic remedy handy had there been one. The whole was so much wind, designed solely to waft the Pearson party into power.
And so it goes on. I have mentioned the fact that we cannot get information. I have referred to the suggestion that unless we knuckle down and pass the kind of legislation that will be introduced in order to implement the plans of this government, we are going to sit all summer. Let me make this perfectly clear; we will not be intimidated in that way. We are not going to pass legislation that we know is going to affect detrimentally the Canadian people, just for the sake of something that every hon. member would like to have and has a right to, a certain vacation during the summertime. We are not going to be intimidated like that.
Now, sir, I said I was not going to speak at length, because I am so anxious to hear what the answer is. The facts are known; they are unchallengeable, and the aroused Canadian people are asking parliament why it cannot get action in this regard and protect them against the proclivities of a government
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]

in its policies that can only adversely affect this country. That being so, sir, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Digby-An-napolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan):
That this house regrets that the government by its failure to clarify many doubts and uncertainties in some of its economic policies has created and continues to create confusion and chaos in various sectors of the economy, thereby contributing to a lamentable slowing down of expected expansion and growth.
I shall pass this to you in a moment, Mr. Speaker, but I wanted the house to know what the amendment was. The doubts remain because every minister of the government sits tight, refuses to answer, refuses to hold out any hope as to what is going to be done. The dribbles here and the dribbles there take away something that has already been directed. There is uncertainty and confusion everywhere. The result is that many of the major sectors of our economy are seriously concerned with this situation. A moment ago I spoke of the construction industry, the building industry, the low production mines; and on the farm and everywhere there is an overwhelming demand by the Canadian people for information and action now, not the kind of thing we have had for 18 or 19 days, uncertainty, moving forward by declaration and then retreating in the face of an aroused public opinion. I know it is going to be hard for them to do it; it is going to be a bitter pill and I do not like to see them in that position.

Not at all; I can feel for you and I want to be entirely fair in that regard. But, sir, the longer they delay swallowing that pill, the more is the economy of Canada being undermined. The government has no other course open to it than to bend in the face of the opposition of this party and of the Canadian people as a whole. Can we get them to do it? Well, I look forward to the great retreat that must come when they rise and find inexplicable reasons for doing this. The hon. gentleman who rose on a question of privilege today said he could not find out the reason some things were done. They will never explain in this case, either, why they have done it.
Sir, when they do it, it will be because they realize that the opposition in this parliament represents the thinking, the general idea, of the Canadian people.

speechtext: Since the hon. gentleman has referred to the motion I made, perhaps I should speak for one minute on this point of order. The hon. member quoted a clause from an amendment I had the honour of moving a few days ago. If the motion before us dealt exclusively with the same matter, I think the hon. member would be fully in order. That is one of the reasons why we did not deal with the budget per se. We are dealing with matters which occurred since that amendment was brought in. We are dealing in today's amendment with the failure of the government to clear up inconsistencies and deal with doubts which have been raised since I moved the amendment. I moved an amendment on the budget. Heaven knows, that was bad enough-I mean the budget. But the uncertainties and doubts which have arisen since then are even worse. We saw a great example this afternoon when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) said that next Monday he would be able to make a statement clarifying something in the budget. We are not attempting here to deal with the budget itself, or with any of the problems arising out of it. We are drawing attention to the failure of the government to deal with questions which have arisen since the budget was brought down.

That in general his proposals will endanger and curtail the expansion of the economy.

-the failure of the government to clarify many doubts and uncertainties in some of its economic policies.
This is a point of difference which Your Honour, I am sure, is taking into account. I wish to thank all hon. members for their assistance in this matter. I have before me the wording of the motion which the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) moved at the time of the budget debate. In particular, paragraph two of that motion reads:
That in general his proposals will endanger and curtail the expansion of the economy.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) raises a very fine distinction, and Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, at page 420, says in part:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion; for instance, a matter already decided by the house, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the orders of the day, cannot be discussed.
The distinction is a very fine distinction indeed. The motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and seconded by the hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), while being very close to the budget motion, does contain a certain element that has to be considered, namely-
-that the government, by its failure to clarify many doubts and uncertainties in some of its economic policies-[DOT]
If we were not about to discuss the budget at some future time this motion would stand on its own feet. Therefore, in the present circumstances I feel that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the opposition in this case and that the motion is in order. The amendment as moved reads:
That this house regrets that the government, by its failure to clarify many doubts and uncertainties in some of its economic policies, has created and continues to create confusion and chaos in various sectors of the economy, thereby contributing to a lamentable slowing down of expected expansion and growth.
May I say in closing that I hope we will be sticking to the "many doubts and uncertainties", rather than indulge at this time in a budget debate.

I agree that the program of the armed forces last night ought to have been seen by every man and woman, every youngster in our country, and I join in commending the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for their performances.
My attention has been drawn to an editorial in the Brantford Expositor dated June 28 dealing with just where the term Dominion of Canada originated. During the conference of the confederation fathers, when they were finalizing the British North America Act, the question came up as to what this united Canada should be called. Sir Leonard Tilley, one of the confederation fathers, went home and spoke to his family about it. The next evening, when picking up his Bible, he turned to the 72nd Psalm and he read these words:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea.
Taking these words back to the confederation conference he mentioned this to those at the conference with him and it was decided then and there that this united Canada should be called the Dominion of Canada. There are those who feel that the word "dominion" may have colonial connotations, but I was impressed with this little story about how the word "dominion" came to be used. Certainly a nation under God, such as Canada is, could not have a more appropriate title than the Dominion of Canada, when it is referred to in the sense that Sir Leonard Tilley originally thought of when he proposed the adoption of this name.
What we need in Canada today more than anything else is a sense of unity, a sense of national purpose. In just four years we will be celebrating our centennial, and I think it is imperative for us in this house, even when we speak in terms of the supply motion, of the expenditure of money or of the carrying on of the administration of government, that we should be thinking a great deal about just what kind of Canada we will have in 1967, and also what kind of a centennial we will provide for this tremendous landmark in our history. Over the week end I was impressed by a letter I received from the secretary of the village council of Bowden, which is in my constituency. It asked me with whom the writer should get in contact in regard to planning our centennial in 1967. People across Canada are looking and groping for leadership in this regard. As I read the July 1 issue of Weekend magazine I read the article concerning a proposition that it might be a good thing to create an eleventh province with the name of Ottawa, which would be a gift from the two larger provinces

I was much impressed by this article written by one of the esteemed members of our press gallery because I think he has a very sound idea, and it was expressed in a way I had not heard before. This article brought the fact clearly to us that we are a nation. What we all ought to be doing in our country, particularly as leaders in our respective spheres, is to concern ourselves about this problem of national unity and purpose. Certainly our financial policies ought to respect the basic premise that brought us into confederation in the first place.
In this regard, one of the most vital things is provincial autonomy in the field of taxation, in the field of carrying forward those things which were promised to the provinces when the provinces came together to form a nation.
I am much disturbed over some of the aspects of the financial policy of the government in this regard. Apparently there is not too much thought or premeditation about how some of the policies which are being introduced will affect the autonomy of the provinces and the relationship of that to the unity that our country needs. Time does not suffice today to deal with this problem at any length.
I doubt that any single event that has taken place in the last months in our country has done so much to jar the Canadian people into thinking about what our future is, particularly as it relates to our financial problems, as the recent budget which has been introduced and the 11 per cent tax which is the basis of the amendment moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). Even though the amendment does not say so in direct terms, the reference obviously is to this 11 per cent tax contained in the budget. The worst blow that industrial growth and expansion of our country have ever been dealt in recent years is this 11 per cent tax. This is just not my opinion; this is the opinion of practically every one of the members sitting in this house, whether they are on this side of the house or on that side.
I have here a file of letters and telegrams which have come in over the week end. Almost universally, there is this shock and amazement that a minority government, such as the present government, should have introduced a policy such as this one. This is not just a response from the Canadian people themselves, but from the construction associations and merchandising associations, as well as from local governments. This response comes from every aspect of Canadian life. Even the press, which only a few short weeks ago was completely behind the present government, has turned harshly in its criticism of the government. The budget was ill


conceived and poorly planned. I do not believe the excuse that there was not time to delve into all the aspects of budget policy is a legitimate excuse. Surely being an expert such as the Minister of Finance, the elementary aspects of these problems which affect the economy could have been dealt with in sufficient detail within a reasonable length of time.
Coming back to this question of provincial rights. I may say that I am concerned, if this is the policy the government is going to follow, about whether or not we should forget about celebrating July 1 and our centenary which we will be celebrating in four years time. We may be celebrating something at that time but we will not be celebrating confederation. It is certainly the responsibility of the Minister of Finance, because of the over-all responsibility of government for planning carefully to take into consideration these matters and to seek the advice which he needs to have if he is not completely aware of all the aspects himself.
One obvious point that has come out of the budget and the tremendous expenditures involved in the estimates before us, is that the present government, at least in so far as its policies so far enunciated are concerned, have been no more able to cope with many of the financial problems of our country than was the former government. What we must understand in this regard is that if the old does not work, if the traditional pattern of the past does not meet our needs, then we ought to have enough common sense to turn to something that does offer an answer.
What is going to happen at the present time in so far as the expressed purposes of the budget are concerned? We are going to find a slow-down in the construction industry. In fact, as I opened my mail this morning I found a clipping from the Edmonton Journal which stated that the sales tax would cut off one thousand jobs in the city in the immediate future. A telegram was received by one of my colleagues a few minutes ago stating that there is a 20 per cent lay-off of construction workers in the city of Medicine Hat. Instead of reducing unemployment, instead of easing off the financial pressures on many of our people who do not have work, we are adding to their number. In addition to that, what is actually being done is to place a penalty against capital investment. This has created confusion throughout the entire economy of our country. Therefore, I urge the Minister of Finance and the government to give immediate consideration to the removal of the 11 per cent tax altogether, or at least to delay the implementation of it.
The other day we had a discussion in the house as to whether or not the Minister of

Finance was planning to define the various fields to which this tax would apply and to which no previous reference had been made. We were given an assurance that this was going to be done. The obvious ramifications of the 11 per cent tax reach out into many more different fields than was originally expected. The situation surrounding this tax can best be characterized as one of confusion and uncertainty which is slowing down instead of speeding up, which is throwing out of work instead of providing new jobs, which is controlling the over-all expansion rather than giving impetus to it. What will happen,
I	sincerely ask the Minister of Finance, if the government does not take this suggestion for removing the tax or delaying its implementation?
The unemployment picture is going to be aggravated and will become a bigger problem than ever before. Capital investment in projects all across the country as related to the expansion of our industry will slow down, because without the construction aspect of industrial expansion you cannot have industrial expansion. Therefore the over-all picture in the country will become more difficult on the economic side than it has been in the past, and the very antithesis of the objective that the Minister of Finance said was his objective when he presented the budget.
Suppose the minister were to listen to the cries of our people across the land and to the advice I am offering at this moment. I think he would find that there would be a way out of the immediate problem that faces us. If there could be a six months' delay in the implementation of the tax a tremendous impetus would be given to over-all industrial expansion throughout the country. You would find that home building would speed up. You would find that industry would instal new machinery and equipment in their plants in order to modernize and expand before the
II	per cent tax was implemented. I think you would find that there would probably be more incentive to go ahead and expand and accomplish what was stated to be the objective of the budget than would be achieved by anything else that could be done.
Therefore I urge once again in the strongest possible way that the government take into consideration the urgency of the matter and at least postpone the implementation of the tax. I think practically all members of the house would agree with such action. What I am saying is not just opposition from the opposition side. These are the facts of the case as they exist in the country today. The government might be placed in a most embarrassing situation by having to backtrack on their declared intentions, but nevertheless it would be better to do that in an

Mr. Speaker, I am not speaking directly to the 11 per cent sales tax. I am speaking of the effects that have been caused as a result of the tax and I am speaking directly to the thought and intent of the wording of the amendment, "to clarify many doubts and uncertainties", proposed by the Leader of the Opposition.
So far as the situation today is concerned, the most urgent matter in the minds of the Canadian people in every province of the nation and every community in every province is how the financial policies of the government are going to affect them. They expected something that at least would not add to their tax burden. They expected something that would give them new hope in order to go forward with the expansion that we all agree we should have in the country.
The doubts and uncertainties created as a result of the financial policies expressed in the budget have truly caused confusion throughout the country and this is of urgent and grave concern to every single one of us. In the motion of supply that is before us today we are actually concerned with the expenditure of millions and millions of dollars which first of all have to be taken out of the taxpayers' pockets before they can be spent. Deeper than any single aspect of the budget, deeper than the 11 per cent tax levied against building materials and equipment and machinery is the fact that the government is not facing up to the basic needs of our economy or to the responsibilities it assumed when it took office. Deeper than this is the simple premise that unless we can get to the root causes of our problem we are going to continue to add to the tax load of our nation, thus taking away the very liberties and freedoms which we regard as basic to our Canadian way of life, and thus defeating the very purpose for which government is intended.
What we should be considering and doing as we speak about this tremendous expenditure of money is discovering ways and means to lighten the tax load so that there will be a more equitable tax on the various segments of the economy without hurting individuals, while at the same time putting into the hands of individuals a greater earning capacity and more dollars with which to purchase the very things that the economy produces. Over and over we in the Social Credit group have emphasized in the house that our real problem is not one of production but rather one of consumption. We have said that in the over-all philosophy of taxation and paying for the cost of government administration the premise must be understood that unless the people have the money in their hands to


buy the things which are made for them and which they want to use, they are not going to have the money to pay the taxes that the government needs to cover the cost of government administration.
That is why I am convinced that unless our government expenditures aim at solving the problems of distribution and consumption, and direct their assistance and guidance in the over-all planning of our economy along that line, we are going to continue to go on from one budget situation to another, typical of the one we have now. It matters not whether a government is called Conservative, Liberal or something else. Unless we can get down to those basic problems and make sure our financial system permits the distribution and consumption of those things we produce, we will never have an answer to the question of how to finance the operations of our government.
That is why we are most concerned in the situation which exists at present. It is not simply a question of collecting dollars out of the taxpayers' pockets to pay for the costs of administration. It also concerns the fairness and the equitableness of taxes as they do this. I find there is a great deal of discrimination developing, simply because there was not the foresight of proper budget planning and because there was not the consultation that there should have been in the preparation of these aspects of the budget. This brings us to the postion that we are in. Instead of talking about some of the major problems on the motion for supply now before us, we are talking about the confusion that exists in every sector of our economy in relation to the 11 per cent sales tax.
Therefore I again urge upon the Minister of Finance and the government that they take immediate action to delay the implementation of their tax policies and face up to the facts as they are, in order that we can have the confidence that our industry and people must have if they are to move forward. The government will admit I am sure, as they have already admitted, that these new taxes were ill conceived and therefore the urgency I am speaking about is of paramount importance.
I do not intend to belabour this point, but I do believe the most urgent matter before the house and the government is to deal with the problem that is posed in the amendment which is before the house, and on which we shall be voting later tonight.
We in the Social Credit party believe that we have a responsibility to those who voted for us and gave us their confidence in the last election. I believe each one of us, no matter what party he belongs to, agrees we

all have that same responsibility. It is our responsibility, as we see it, in the light of the tremendous expression that has been voiced. I wish to emphasize again that we cannot continue this policy, which has brought us to the point where we are now. Therefore I again ask the Minister of Finance to clarify the various problems facing the many aspects of industry today as a result of this sales tax, and I urge him once more to at least delay the implementation of the tax until a later date.

Mr. Speaker, the motion to go into supply always provides an opportunity for the opposition, on the one hand, to bring forth any criticism it has of the general direction in which the government is going, and it provides the government, on the other hand, with an opportunity to explain to the house and the country how far it has gone in carrying out the program with which it began its term in office.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has directed his remarks mainly to the economic plight of Canada, and I think he did well to do this because this is undoubtedly the problem which gives the greatest concern to the people of the country. From 1957 to 1961 our gross national product increased something less than 2 per cent per year, when we put it into constant dollars and make adjustment for price changes. Last year we made a much more substantial increase in our gross national product, but it was mainly in the extraction industries and it did not reflect itself in a decrease in unemployment. In the first quarter of this year our gross national product increased about 1 per cent over the last quarter of 1962.
There is no need to weary the house with statistics. I think every member of the house who has studied this matter will agree that, whether we all have the same figures to a decimal point or not, the inescapable fact is that our economy for the past six years has not been increasing at a rate which will provide full employment not only for those who are now employable but also for the 200,000 or more young people who enter the labour market each year, and that the main task facing this parliament, and particularly facing the government, is how we can promote the type of economic growth that will soak up the pool of unemployment which has remained at an average of about 6.6 per cent per year, and at the same time provide jobs for the growing army of young people entering the labour market.
The government started off on April 22 with many cheers and a fanfare of trumpets as to what it was going to do about promoting
Alleged Confusion in Economic Policies economic growth and providing full employment. But now, shortly after the 60 days have expired, we have come to the point where it seems to have slowed down and run out of steam. Some of the measures it has brought in are already being greeted with less enthusiasm by hon. members opposite than when they were introduced. I make particular reference, for instance, to the municipal development and loan board, a piece of legislation which in principle has much to commend it; but the government seems to be losing its enthusiasm for it, and certainly some of the government's supporters outside the house have openly criticized it.
The reason why so much of its legislation has not been widely acclaimed is due to the fact that there has not been the kind of consultation which there ought to have been before the legislation was introduced. This is particularly true where the legislation involves the provinces. I can give just a minor matter as an illustration.
The government announced very sweeping changes in its winter works incentive program, something which vitally affects the provinces. As a matter of fact the provinces do much of the work, but I know of one province where the deputy minister was phoned at 4.30 in the afternoon and told, "We propose to make these changes. Will you discuss them with your minister, have him discuss them with the cabinet and call us back tomorrow morning?" When he called back next morning at 10.30 o'clock he was told, "Sorry, it has gone through cabinet." I am all for haste and doing business expeditiously, but if the government expects to get the cooperation of the provinces, not only on minor matters but on much larger matters, it will have to carry on a great deal more consultation than has been evident to date. This is true of consultation with industry, with labour, with agriculture and with other segments of the economy. Much of the trouble which the government is experiencing today could have been avoided had there been consultation with those who were affected by the various pieces of legislation that have been brought down.
It seems to me there has been a lack of planning, a lack of a sense of direction. The government has talked a great deal about regaining control of the economy but it does not seem to have any program or philosophy by which Canada is going to regain control of its economy. It talks glibly about trade, but we have had no statement yet from the government, after having been in session since May 16, as to what its trade program is. Here is Canada, a country that lives by trade; here is a nation that must export or perish, and yet not a word in any legislation or in

the budget as to what the government proposes to do about Canada's place as a great trading power.
I think the main reason the government's economic policy seems to have collapsed in midstream is that it has never yet got down to the base causes of the economic malaise that has been affecting the Canadian economy. They have been dealing with fringe problems; they have never got down to the basic problems.
I am not going to repeat what I have said on previous occasions, but the basic problems for the last five or six years have not been the lack of savings by industry or the lack of profit incentives, because profits have been good. The basic lack in the Canadian economy has been the lack of effective purchasing power in the hands of a great segment of the Canadian population. We contend that the answer lies in doing two things: First, introducing great quantities of purchasing power into the economy by government action, by large scale public works programs and large scale housing programs. Immediately this raises the whole question of deficit financing, and yet modern economists in countries where they have studied deficit financing tell us that in the main, for every percentage point that a country reduces its unemployment figures it increases its gross national product by 3 per cent. This means that if we could reduce Canada's unemployment figure to an annual average of 3 per cent-and this would still be higher than any country in western Europe-we could increase Canada's gross national product by over $4,000 million a year. This is the answer to those who become concerned about deficit financing.
I would have thought that in the first 60 days the first thing the government would have done would have been to announce large scale federal public works projects, large scale housing programs and financial assistance to enable the provinces to embark upon provincial public works programs. They have-let it be said, so I am perfectly fair- introduced legislation by which they will assist municipalities to embark upon socially useful public works; it may be not on as large a scale as might be desired, but they have made a commendable start. But there has been nothing federally, nothing provincially to launch the kind of large scale public works projects that are absolutely necessary in order to put men to work until such time as the economy itself is able to absorb these people in ordinary, everyday enterprises. This is why, in the opinion of this group, reimposing the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery was such an erroneous step.
I am not going to discuss this tax; I simply use it by way of illustration. This 
tax has been imposed at the very time when this country ought to be booming, when we ought to be putting men to work in the logging camps, the saw mills, the cement factories, the brick factories, when the various forms of transportation ought to be hauling building materials, when construction workers should be busy, when we should be building homes, apartment blocks, office blocks, libraries, recreation centres, hospitals, schools; when we ought to be building federal and provincial parks, irrigation projects. When we should be doing these things is not the time-in fact, it is the very last time-to be applying an 11 per cent sales tax.
The other thing that must be done, in addition to large scale public works, is to use every economic device at the disposal of the government to redistribute purchasing power to those in our economy who would, if they had more money, buy more consumer goods. This is self-evident. This means increasing old age pensions and veterans pensions; it means lowering the age for the old age pensioners to 65; it means raising the family allowances and raising the age to 18 for children who go to school; it means leaving the people in the lower income groups with more money in their pockets by raising the exemptions or lowering the income tax on these groups. Again, this is the very time not to have introduced a sales tax, because a sales tax is a regressive tax. At the present time the government of Canada collects about 60 per cent of its taxes directly, and 40 per cent indirectly; but when the average taxpayer pays his provincial and municipal taxes, which have to be weighted in the form of direct taxes, he is paying about 50 per cent as direct taxes and 50 per cent as indirect. The thing that is wrong with indirect taxes is that they take no cognizance whatsoever of the individual's ability to pay. Therefore the pendulum is swinging more and more toward indirect taxes rather than direct taxes. If ever there was a time in our economy when we ought to be reducing sales taxes and, if we have to have revenue, get it from those who are better able to pay, this was the time; not just on humanitarian grounds but on the grounds of good economics, because every $100 that people in low income groups save by not having to pay them in taxes will be used to buy consumer goods and so help stimulate the economy. That is very simple Keynesian economics which is being practised in most of the modern countries of the world. One of the ways in which we could help to redistribute purchasing power would be by putting more money in the pockets of the farm population. One of the ways in which we could best redistribute purchasing power would be by guaranteeing

parity prices to the primary producers, the farmers, the fishermen and others in this country who produce these basic commodities. There is probably no group which has suffered more during this period of economic stagnation than the farming population, because the farming population have to buy in a protected market and sell on the world market. Since 1951 they have found that though the prices they pay for the things they have to buy have risen by 24 per cent, the prices of the goods they sell have gone down by 21 per cent.
I have here the quarterly bulletin of agriculture put out by the dominion bureau of statistics, national accounts, covering the period from January to March, 1962 and comparing it with other years. We find that in 1951 the average income per farm was $3,250. By 1958 that had dropped to $2,558. In 1959, it was $2,659, in 1960 it was up to $2,999 and in 1961 it had dropped again to $2,393. Income for 1962 will be a little higher because that was a very good crop year. But the trend is the same; the trend is that income from agriculture has tended to decline, and the farmer, because he does not control his market, is not able to keep the prices of his products in line with his cost of production. His cost of production has gone up while in many cases the prices he receives for his commodities have gone down.
During the election campaign the Liberal party made many promises about what they intended to do for the farmer. The most specific promise was made with respect to the wheat farmers. I have here a copy of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 7 reporting a speech of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the leader of the Liberal party. The heading is: "Two Price Wheat System" and it says:
A two price system for wheat to recognize the farm price-cost squeeze was promised by Liberal leader Pearson here Wednesday night in an address to the largest rally of his current election campaign held in the arena. Mr. Pearson said it would replace the "present haphazard system of acreage payments the government can give whenever it decides to" and would "eject stability in the farming industry so that farmers could plan ahead." Speaking from a prepared text, Mr. Pearson said his party if elected, would immediately establish a floor price of $2 per bushel for No. 1 Northern at Fort William to give "a measure of security to the wheat producer."
This price would apply over the life of the present international wheat agreement. A two price system would be legislated on the basis of the unit quota. "Farmers will be paid a price for wheat used in domestic human consumption which reflects the fact they buy their production requirements in tariff-protected markets and sell in world markets", he said. It would be accompanied by a consumer subsidy so that bread prices wouldn't rise.

No one can say this was just a passing reference. This was a major speech made by the leader of the Liberal party in one of the largest cities on the prairies and it constitutes a definite commitment to the wheat growers of western Canada that if a Liberal government were elected, two things would happen: first, there would be a two price system for wheat, so that wheat used for domestic purposes would be bought at a parity price, the money being paid to the farmers on the basis of certain delivery quotas and, second that there would be a guaranteed price of $2 a bushel so that if the price of wheat sold under the international wheat agreement were to drop below $2, the government would make up the difference.
That was the commitment. Whether it is done this way, or whether it is done by parity prices, the value of such a program is that it would put purchasing power into the pockets of the primary producers of this country. If the farmers and fishermen of Canada could have the benefit of parity prices, prices which give them a fair return for their production in relation to their costs, they would be in a position to buy consumer goods in tremendous quantities. I know of nothing which would give the economy a greater stimulus than to put parity prices into operation for the primary producers of this country. That is why we have always contended that parity prices are not only a matter of social justice but that they make economic good sense because they would enable the great primary producing groups in our country to buy larger and ever larger quantities of consumer goods. If the government would keep even its own promise of a $2 a bushel guarantee for wheat and a two price system, a burst of purchasing power would be liberated which would give our economy such a shot in the arm that many of our economic problems would disappear.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) has moved an amendment, and I do not disagree with the terms of the amendment that the government has failed to clarify many doubts and uncertainties in some of its economic policies and that it has created, and continues to create, confusion and chaos in various sectors of the economy, thereby contributing to a lamentable slowing down of expected expansion and growth. While this amendment calls attention to the lack of clarification and to the confusion which exists, it does not suggest any remedy. It is in this respect that I disagree with the amendment. I think we must do more than criticize the government for its lack of clarification, for its confusion and lack of direction. I think we must also place before the house some concrete measures which we think should be
1748	HOUSE OF
Alleged Confusion in Economic Policies taken to give this economy a new sense of direction, a new impetus, to help promote economic growth and put unemployed people to work; to provide adequate social welfare, and to give the primary producers of this country a standard of living which is in keeping with that enjoyed by other segments of the economy.
Therefore I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after the word "government" and by substituting therefor the following words:
-has failed to Introduce the kind of economic planning that would promote economic growth and full employment, and more particularly has failed to institute a large scale program of housing and public works, to create more effective consumer demand, and to introduce a system of parity prices for primary products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity to speak, if not about the budget at least about certain emanations from it. A lot has happened in the last three weeks and the public, and even, perhaps, some hon. members of this house may have become confused to some extent by the side issues, the

alarms and the excursions. The amendment before the house is worded in the most general terms. In my remarks I shall try to point out not only the broad problems that confront the country but I shall also say something about the issue that was clearly in the mind of the right hon. gentleman opposite who moved the amendment, namely the withdrawal of the sales tax exemption from certain industries. It seems to me that in view of the wording of the amendment and in view of the wide ranging remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker)
I should be entitled to this latitude.
Let me begin by reminding hon. members that the tax in question is one which a great many other industries have been paying for many years. The withdrawal of the exemption will place most industries-and I should explain that I mean most industries excepting food-on the same basis. The sales tax imposed by the Excise Tax Act is usually referred to as a general manufacturers sales tax. It is imposed on the manufacturer or producer and the amount of the tax is a percentage of the manufacturer's or producer's selling price. It also applies to imports: in this case it is paid by the importer or the person who takes the goods out of bond for consumption, and the tax is a percentage of the duty paid value of the imported article.
The tax is called a single stage tax, as opposed to a turnover type of tax. This means it is applied only once as goods pass from manufacturer to final user. This is done by a system of licensing. The reason I am explaining this, Mr. Speaker, is that there seems to be some misunderstanding on how this tax works. Those who are licensed must pay the tax on sales to unlicensed purchasers. Those who are licensed buy the materials to be wrought into goods they manufacture free of sales tax under their licence. For example, the manufacturer of shoes buys leather free of sales tax; he must pay sales tax on the selling price of the finished shoes when he sells them to an unlicensed wholesaler or retailer. Although the sales tax is imposed on the manufacturer or importer, it is usual for him to include the tax in his selling price; thus the user of taxable goods bears the tax in the form of the higher price he must pay for the goods.
The sales tax is a general tax; that is, it applies to all goods sold or imported for consumption in Canada except those made exempt by the Excise Tax Act. The exemptions may be in the form of listing articles to be exempt-for example, the act lists most foodstuffs-or the exemption may be in the form of providing that all goods purchased by certain purchasers shall be exempt. For example, purchases by hospitals or provincial

governments are exempt. The sales tax is imposed at the rate of 8 per cent under the Excise Tax Act and 3 per cent under the Old Age Security Act; that is, three elevenths of the revenue from the sales tax goes to help pay for old age pensions.
I should like to remind hon. members once again of some of the problems that confront this country. We are committed-and when I say this, I naturally mean the government is committed-to a fixed exchange rate for the Canadian dollar. In my opinion it would be the height of irresponsibility to contemplate a second major devaluation of the currency. This government has stated that it will support the fixed rate for the dollar. In so doing we know that this limits our room for manoeuvre very greatly. The second question or issue that I would like to remind hon. members of is that the levels of interest rates in Canada are considerably lower than they were some months ago, and this should help all segments of the economy. It would be pleasant if interest rates could be reduced still further, but given a fixed exchange rate for the dollar and given the rates of interest that prevail across the line, there are clear limits to what can be done in this connection.
Surely we are all aware of the chronic deficits in our current account payments with other countries; we know that this is at the root of many of our problems. When I say that, I naturally include unemployment, which is the greatest problem of them all. We know that firm action will be needed on many fronts if we are to resolve this particular problem. During the election campaign we on this side undertook to begin to put our house in order, to begin to work toward a balanced budget. Accomplishing this objective means cutting expenditures wherever this is feasible, and the government is initiating, as I said some time ago, a close review of all existing programs to see what can be done on this account. At the same time, additional revenues must be secured if the objective of moving toward a budgetary balance is to be achieved. To listen to the debates in this house one would think that Canadians had no real idea of the trouble we are in, of the absolute necessity of doing something about our present situation.

I do not like the proposed sales tax any more than anybody else does, but some substantial increase in government revenues is absolutely necessary. So I say to the critics of this tax; just what are the alternatives? Members of the New Democratic party say we should do nothing. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) would like to see our budgetary deficits increased. He argues that if consumer expenditures are increased this will in turn increase the general level of economic activity throughout the country. I say to him that the trouble with this theory as applied to Canada-and I say this with respect, because I am not unaware of the theory; I understand it, I think-is that about one quarter of such increased expenditure, or so it is estimated, would find its way into additional imports of one kind or another and this would aggravate our payments problem and only add to our difficulties in the long run.
It is not good enough to suggest a simple formula without understanding all its implications in the circumstances in which Canada finds herself at the moment. I say to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and to other hon. members, that we shall not gain anything by burying our heads in the sand and hoping our problems will get up and go away. That is not going to happen.
Now let me say a word about the need for additional revenues and about the decision to impose this particular tax instead of the alternatives which we considered. If no additional tax were imposed this year, the budget deficit would exceed $700 million, as I said in the course of the budget speech. Next year, the deficit would be much larger still after taking into account, first, the substantial tax incentives which were proposed in the budget and which, I suggest, will have more to do with the reinvigoration of the depressed or surplus manpower areas in this country than anything else which has ever been presented in this house; second, the cost of the government's new programs when they are brought into being, as I hope and expect they will be, eventually; third, the cost involved in clearing up some of the things which have to be cleared up, such as the deficit in the unemployment fund and, fourth, the cost of taking into account increased expenditures of various kinds including pay increases which are overdue. It would not take a very sharp pencil to calculate that the budget deficit
