Four or five alternatives were considered, with a view to raising between $300 millions and $400 millions of additional revenue in a full year's operation. The first of these was an increase across the board in the present sales tax. However, I would remind hon. members that a 4 per cent increase in the present sales tax, which should produce about $400 million of additional revenue in a full year, given the levels of production and prices prevailing at the present time, would mean applying increases to such things as clothing, books and shoes, house furnishings, furniture, household appliances and so on. If the existing sales tax were increased it would add directly to the cost of living of those who are least able to afford it, and it was for this reason that this course was discarded by the government.
The second course which was open to us- and it was certainly considered carefully- was a general increase in the rates of personal income tax. Nothing substantial can be achieved by increasing only the rates of those in the higher income bracket. There just is not enough to begin in that area. If this course were to produce the kind of additional revenues which we need it would have been necessary to increase the income in all brackets by somewhere between 20 and 25 per cent. This would have meant an increase in the annual tax in the case of a single person with a monthly income of $250 of between $47 and $59. It would have meant an increase in the tax of a married man with no dependants and a monthly income of $350 a month of between $53 and $67. I should perhaps add, if any hon. members are interested, that the 25 per cent increase in all rates would have brought the top rate above the 100 per cent mark. A 20 per cent increase in the rates of personal income tax would have produced about $310 million additional revenue to the federal government in the year 1964-65. A 25 per cent increase across the board would have produced about $385 million for the federal authorities in the year 1964-65. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, personal income tax rates are already much too high. The thought of increasing them, especially in the lower income brackets, is abhorrent and for this reason this course was also discarded.
Just in passing, people have asked me why we did not increase the tax on luxuries- cigarettes, alcohol, and that sort of thing. The answer is very simple. If you put the tax past a certain point the net revenues decline; they do not go up. This has been tried before.


The third serious course was to consider the rates of corporation income taxes and to see if these could be increased; but an increase of 5 per cent on taxable income would have produced only about $200 million in a full year. Furthermore, this would have placed the rates in Canada substantially above those which prevail across the line, and because, as we all know, of the interrelationship of so many Canadian and American companies, the net result would have been to slow down business activity in Canada very quickly. The rates are already 52 per cent and it would have meant putting them away above that. Instead the government has proposed that corporate income tax payments be put on the same basis as individual income tax payments, and in this way there will be additional revenues collected next year amounting to some $200 million.
Finally, the fourth serious alternative open to the government, having turned down the various courses to which I have referred, was to impose what I consider a very tough tax that falls on those undertaking capital projects and on industry in general. We could have taken a course which would have resulted in a substantial increase in taxes for the small man and thus have avoided the heavy pressures-and I should like to say that they are quite legitimate and proper pressures, but nevertheless they are heavy- from the businessmen who will be hurt by the tax that has been imposed. There is an old saying, Mr. Speaker, about a certain road which is paved with good intentions and I think the Minister of Finance must have been travelling that road. The only difference is that now because of the sales tax on building material he will have to pay a lot more for the material he will have to use to pave that road than he would have before.
The minister referred to the tax on building materials, but that is only one facet, even though it is a most important one from the standpoint of the whole nation. Almost every individual is faced with an increased tax, in building and in repairing. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I have had letters and representations with respect to repairs, and there is no $500 contribution for that work. If a man repairs or paints his house this tax will add to his cost. My colleague, the former minister of labour, had a slogan, "Do it now", which was to encourage people to undertake works in winter time. Now the slogan of the government is, "Don't do it at all" because it is going to cost so much more money.


This tax on building materials is a very important matter which we will deal with at length when the resolution is before us, but it is only one of a score of matters to which reference has been made.
I think some hon. members have seen copies of a number of briefs which have come to us within the last few days. I myself saw one today from the Canadian graphic arts association, the organization representing members of the graphic arts industry, which is of course a very wide and large one in this country. Now the minister says there are difficult questions, and when you bring in something new you are bound to get some doubts and some indecision. I suggest when something new is brought in that is going to create doubts and indecision then more careful study should be given to it before it is brought in, and certainly more than has been the case in this budget. Had the Minister of Finance spent less time, on the occasion of bringing in his budget, on political vituperation and more on explanations perhaps the nation would not have the problems which it faces now.
Looking over the brief which was submitted by the graphic arts organization we find some of the most interesting statements set forth concerning things that you would no believe possible in a government in a country which was newly organized. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to reflect on any government, but if some of these things were found, for instance, in the Congolese parliament under the premiership of Mr. Lumumba, who died an untimely death some years ago, you would not believe it possible.
For example we find that the president of this association met with officers of the Department of National Revenue. Mr. Speaker, I know something of those officers. I have worked with them for four or five years, and I think all hon. members will agree we have a very experienced and very able group of officers in that department. Indeed I was often amazed, during the days when I was closely associated with them, to pose the most difficult and intricate questions to them, involving the administration of the finance act and to get almost immediate answers to my questions. But the president of the graphic arts association says that, 13 days after the budget was brought down, he put 32 questions to the officers of the Department of National Revenue, specific questions asking for specific answers to specific problems with which the industry was confronted, and to one third of those questions the senior officers said they could give no answer whatsoever. Then the government has the nerve to talk about decision in a situation such as that.

One of the corporations confronted with this tax asked for a ruling from the department, and the department replied, "If we will give you a tentative ruling"-I am paraphrasing now-"we are not sure it is right; we are not sure that the Department of Justice will approve of it; we are not sure we can make it stick; but if we can, and if we decide to give you a ruling you will be paying tax on $40,000 worth of product. That will be the figure. But if we don't give you that ruling you are going to pay the tax on $1,400,000 worth of product." What a situation with which to confront only one of scores of hundreds of producers. That is the problem they are confronted with tonight, and that is 19 days after the budget was brought down. The brief ends up by saying that the industry is in a total state of confusion. Many of its firms have their financial year ending on June 30 and they do not know how to close their books.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there are many firms in this country tonight sending out invoices which are following a very easy practice, but one which is going to lead to great confusion. They bill the purchaser for the costs, whatever they may be, and on the bottom they state "To be added, whatever tax the government decides to impose." There are scores, hundreds and thousands of invoices being sent out like that, and that is one example of the indecision which the Leader of the Opposition referred to this afternoon.
One could go on dealing with the problems facing our industries, but I do not intend to speak at any great length tonight. Whether it is the building industry, the construction industry, the graphic arts industry or almost any other industry, you will find there is a state of confusion resting in the minds of the people tonight and that, Mr. Speaker, is not because of the budget itself. It is because of the lack of care and preparation in the presentation of it, and the absolute indecision and confusion which follows on having people draft it who did not know how to draft it, and when they did draft it, did not know what they were doing.
To turn to another area to which no great reference is made, because one does not always have too great a sympathy with people engaged in financial transactions in the market and so on, we have had a semiwithdrawal, a placing in cold storage or in the mortuary of the 30 per cent takeover tax. How are you going to determine, if you have 25 per cent shareholders today whether you will have the same tomorrow? What are you going

No one in Canada today can tell that. We have sat here very patiently on this side of the house since May 16 allowing practically all the debating to be done by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the house, but we do not appear to have made a great deal of progress in this house by that method. It has occurred to me that if one or two speeches are made from this side of the house, perhaps of a slightly higher quality, but of the same partisan character as the hon. gentlemen opposite make, it might conduce to more progress. On May 2, 1962 the government of that day were driven to devaluation and to pegging the dollar because they had refused to face up to the economic realities which faced this country in the world, and because other countries had lost confidence in our currency.
